title: MLB Arbitration Salary Analysis
text:
Project Overview
This project uses arbitration salary data and pitching performance metrics to estimate which factors most influence first-year arbitration salaries.
The goal is to connect econometric modeling with a real baseball operations question: how players are valued during the arbitration process.

title: MLB Arbitration Salary Analysis
text:
Data

Salary data: Spotrac
Performance data: Fangraphs / Statcast
Sample: First-year arbitration and Super Two starting pitchers
Years: 2016–2026
Observations: 124 pitchers

title: MLB Arbitration OLS Model
text:
Model
I estimated an OLS regression using log salary as the dependent variable.
Independent variables included:

Innings Pitched (IP)
Strikeout Rate (K%)
Walk Rate (BB%)
ERA
Year fixed effects

The logarithmic specification allows coefficients to be interpreted approximately as percentage changes in salary and helps address right-skewness in arbitration salary distributions.
The model estimated how pitcher performance metrics were associated with arbitration outcomes while controlling for season-level differences.

title: MLB Arbitration OLS Model
text:
Key Findings

Workload was strongly rewarded in arbitration.
10 additional innings pitched were associated with roughly a 5.8% increase in salary.
ERA remained highly influential.
One additional run of ERA was associated with roughly an 11% decrease in salary.
Strikeout rate showed moderate evidence of positive salary impact.
The model underpredicted elite performers such as Shane Bieber, Corbin Burnes, and Hunter Brown.

title: MLB Arbitration OLS Model
text:
Baseball Interpretation
The results suggest that first-year arbitration salaries still reward traditional indicators such as innings pitched and ERA.
This matters because arbitration is not just a pure projection system. It reflects performance, precedent, role, reputation, and comparable-player arguments.

title: MLB Arbitration OLS Model
text:
Limitations
Important omitted variables may include:

WAR
Awards
Injuries
Role changes
Reputation
Comparable-player effects
Team/player negotiation context

title: MLB Arbitration Salary Analysis
text:
Next Steps
Future work will focus on:

Residual Analysis to identify overpaid and underpaid arbitration outcomes.
Building comparable-player groups for arbitration forecasting.
Expanding the predictor set to include metrics such as WAR and Stuff+.
Compare linear models with machine learning approaches such as Random Forests and Gradient Boosting.

title: MLB Arbitration Salary Analysis
text:
Sample Summary

124 first-year arbitration and Super-Two starting pitchers.
Salary range: approximately $800K-$8M+.
Average Salary: $2.89M
Average Innings Pitched: 132.1
Average ERA: 3.96

title: MLB Arbitration Salary Analysis
text:
Methodology
I used two complementary modeling approaches:

Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression to estimate the relationship between performance metrics and arbitration salary.
LASSO regularization to identify the most influential predictors and reduce model complexity.

Both models used first-year arbitration and Super-Two starting pitchers from 2016-2026.

title: MLB Arbitration Salary Analysis
text:
LASSO Variable Selection
To complement the OLS model, I applied LASSO regularization with cross-validation to identify the optimal penalty parameter (λ) and determine which variables consistently contribute to salary predictions.
The objective was to determine which pitching metrics consistently contributed to salary predictions while shrinking less informative variables toward zero.

title: MLB Arbitration Salary Analysis
text:
Model Findings

Innings Pitched was the strongest predictor of first-year arbitration salary.
ERA remained a significant measure of run prevention and salary value.
Strikeout rate retained predictive value after controlling for workload and ERA.
Walk rate contributed less explanatory power than other performance metrics.
LASSO variable selection confirmed innings pitched and ERA as the most influential predictors.
Season fixed effects captured changes in arbitration salary environments over time.

title: MLB Arbitration Salary Analysis
text:
Baseball Operations Application
This framework can be used to:

Estimate expected arbitration salaries for eligible players.
Identify potentially overvalued and undervalued arbitration cases.
Support player acquisition and roster construction decisions.
Evaluate comparable-player arguments used during negotiations.
Quantify how traditional and modern performance metrics influence salary outcomes.
